Android from the foundation · Puzzle 15 · 16 of 20

Frames, jank and ANRs

Drawing the screen is just another message in the main thread's queue. So one slow message doesn't only delay a tap: it stops the screen from being drawn.

Builds on: open one to see the idea this puzzle uses.

  • Puzzle 12: Starting an app, cold, warm and hot

    Cold start = fork Zygote, create your Application, then the first Activity. Warm = process alive, Activity created again. Hot = both alive, just brought to the front.

Starting from zero? The blocks under this puzzle are 10 puzzles: 0 → 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 6 → 8 → 10 → 12. Know them already? Start here.

The problem

In puzzle 14, the main thread ran messages one at a time. Now suppose one message takes a long time, like reading a big file, or a Thread.sleep(6000) in a button's click code, which pauses the thread for 6 seconds. What does the user see?

See it

Save this diagram as a GIF

The building block

The screen is redrawn about 60 times a second. Each redraw is a frame, and each one must be ready within about 16 milliseconds (1000 ms ÷ 60). Drawing a frame is a message in the main thread's queue too.

If a message takes longer than that, the frames behind it come late, and the app visibly stutters: jank.

system_server sent each touch down the window's input channel (puzzle 14), and waits for your app to answer "done" on that same line, which it does once the main thread has handled the touch. If a touch waits in the queue for 5 seconds with no answer, system_server shows the "App isn't responding" dialog: an ANR (Application Not Responding). That's why slow work (files, network, big calculations) belongs on another thread, never on the main thread.

The analogy

The clerk also has to repaint the shop window 60 times a second. One long phone call, and the window freezes; keep a customer waiting long enough, and the town hall puts up a sign: "not responding".

Check yourself

A button's click code calls Thread.sleep(6000), and the user taps the screen again right away. What happens?

Not quite. Touches are messages for the main thread too, so they wait behind the sleeping click code.

Right. One message at a time: the touch waits behind the sleep, and after 5 seconds comes the ANR.

Not quite. Nothing is stopped: system_server shows a dialog and the user decides.

A message takes 100 ms (about six frames' worth: 100 ÷ 16), and there are no touches. Is that an ANR?

Right. 100 ms ÷ 16 ms ≈ 6 frames late: jank. A touch waiting 5 s means an ANR.

Not quite. An ANR is about a touch waiting 5 seconds. 100 ms is jank: late frames.

Why should file reading go on another thread?

Not quite. It can; it just mustn't, because frames and touches wait behind it.

Right. Keep every main-thread message short.

Sources

  • Android Developers: Slow rendering (jank)
  • AOSP: InputChannel.java ("An input channel specifies the file descriptors used to send input events to a window in another process") and InputEventReceiver.java (finishInputEvent(event, handled))
  • Android Developers: ANRs

What you now know

A frame is due about every 16 ms. A message that takes longer makes frames late: jank. A touch that waits 5 seconds gets the "App isn't responding" dialog: an ANR.
